h1: Working at a malt house or hop supplier instead of a brewery
title: Careers at Malt Houses and Hop Suppliers | Craft Beer School
desc: The jobs behind the brewery: careers in malting and hop supply, what the work involves and the skills that carry over from brewing.
teaser: Every brewery depends on malt and hops. The people who make and sell them have careers of their own, often with steadier hours.
standfirst: Not every brewing career happens in a brewery. Maltsters, hop merchants and ingredient suppliers employ technical people too. Here is what those jobs look like and why they suit some brewers better than the brewhouse.
sections:
Brewing starts long before mash in. Barley is grown, cleaned, steeped, germinated and kilned into malt. Hops are grown, harvested, dried, pelletised and stored cold. Yeast is propagated and shipped. Each step has its own industry with its own technical and commercial roles.

For someone who loves the science of brewing but not the shift work, or who wants a career path in a larger organisation, the supply side is worth a serious look.

Malting turns barley into a raw material a brewer can use. Grain is steeped in water until it reaches around 42 to 46 percent moisture, germinated for several days while enzymes develop, then kilned to dry it and set its colour and flavour. Our guide to the barley malting process walks through each stage.

Jobs in a malt house include:

  • Production and shift roles running steeping, germination and kilning, often on a 24 hour cycle.
  • Quality and lab roles testing moisture, extract, colour, protein, friability and enzyme activity, then producing the certificate of analysis that goes to each customer.
  • Grain procurement working with farmers and traders on barley quality, variety and price.
  • Technical sales helping brewers choose malts and solve brewhouse problems.

India grows barley mainly in the north and north west, in states such as Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Haryana, Punjab and Madhya Pradesh. Much of the malting industry sits near those growing regions.
Hop supply: a smaller, more commercial world

Commercial hop growing in India is negligible, so nearly all hops used here are imported from countries such as Germany, the Czech Republic, the US, New Zealand and Australia. Hop supply jobs in India are therefore mostly commercial and technical rather than agricultural: importing, cold storage, logistics and helping brewers choose varieties.

A hop sales or technical role means understanding alpha acids, oil content, crop year variation and storage. You explain to a brewer why this year's lot of a variety has different alpha acid from last year's. Then you explain how to adjust the recipe. Abroad, hop merchants and growers also employ people in breeding, agronomy and processing.
A morning in a malt house lab

A lab technician's day often starts with samples from every kiln that finished overnight. Moisture comes first, because malt that leaves the kiln too wet will not store well. Then come the slower tests: extract from a small laboratory mash, wort colour, soluble nitrogen and friability, which shows how well the grain broke down during germination.

Each result is compared with the customer's specification. A batch that misses goes to a different customer or gets blended. The lab is where a maltster keeps its promises, which is why lab experience is respected across the industry.

Brewers moving into supply bring something suppliers value: they know how the ingredient behaves in a brewhouse. A technical sales person who has battled a stuck lauter can tell whether the cause is the malt's modification or the customer's mill gap. A hop specialist who has dry hopped at scale can discuss hop creep and aroma loss in the customer's own terms.

The reverse is also true. Time at a maltster or hop supplier makes you a better brewer if you return, because you understand the specification sheets and the natural variation behind them.

Malt house production suits people who like process control and steady routines, though it is shift work. Lab roles suit careful analysts. Procurement suits people who enjoy negotiation, data and relationships with growers. Technical sales suits people who like travel, problem solving and talking to brewers.

Hours are often more regular than in a brewpub, especially in lab, procurement and sales roles. Career ladders can also be clearer in a larger company, with routes into quality management, operations or commercial leadership.

Employers look for a science or engineering background plus a working knowledge of brewing, because the customer is always a brewer. Learn to read a malt certificate of analysis and to explain what each number means on brew day. Learn the main hop families and how alpha acid drives bitterness calculations.

Most of all, understand the full brewing process, so you can see your ingredient through the customer's eyes. Our guide to jobs in a brewery shows the brewery roles you would be serving.
faqs: Yes, especially for quality, technical sales and customer support roles, where brewing experience helps explain how malt performs in the brewhouse.
Is hop growing a career option in India?
Commercial hop growing in India is negligible, so hop jobs here are mostly in importing, storage, logistics and technical sales rather than farming.
What qualifications do malting jobs need?
A degree in food technology, agriculture, microbiology, chemistry or engineering is common. Brewing and malting courses help you understand the customer's process.
